function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

    57|
    58|## Why This Book Exists
    59|
    60|You're a small business owner. You wear multiple hats—CEO, marketer, salesperson, customer service rep, bookkeeper, and sometimes janitor.     65|
    66|## What You'll Learn
    67|
    68|In the following pages, we'll walk through practical, step-by-step approaches to implementing AI in your small business. You'll discover how to:
    69|
    70|- Save 10+ hours per week on repetitive tasks
    71|- Improve customer satisfaction and retention
    72|- Make data-driven decisions without needing an analytics degree
    73|- Compete more effectively with larger competitors
    74|- Scale your operations without proportional increases in workload or costs
    75|
    76|Each chapter includes real-world case studies from small businesses just like yours, plus hands-on exercises you can implement immediately. By the end of this book, you'll have a customized AI implementation plan tailored to your specific business needs.
    77|
    78|## The AI Advantage for Small Business
    79|
    80|Before you start evaluating AI tools, you need a clear picture of what this technology can actually do for you — and more importantly, what it can't. Too many business owners waste money on AI expecting miracles, or ignore it entirely because they don't understand the real capabilities. This list sets the record straight so you can spot genuine opportunities without falling for hype. Use it as your reality check: if a tool promises something from the "AI CANNOT" list, walk away.
    81|
    82|Let's be clear about what AI can and cannot do for your business:
    83|
    84|**AI CAN:**
    85|- Automate repetitive, time-consuming tasks
    86|- Analyze large amounts of data quickly to uncover patterns
    87|- Provide 24/7 customer support through chatbots
    88|- Personalize marketing messages at scale
    89|- Optimize inventory and supply chain management
    90|- Predict trends and forecast demand
    91|- Enhance decision-making with data-driven insights
    92|
    93|**AI CANNOT:**
    94|- Replace human creativity and emotional intelligence
    95|- Make ethical judgments or value-based decisions
    96|- Understand context the way humans do (yet)
    97|- Function without quality data and proper setup
    98|- Solve poorly defined business problems
    99|
   100|The most successful AI implementations in small businesses don't try to replace humans—they augment human capabilities, freeing you and your team to focus on what you do best: building relationships, solving complex problems, and growing your business.
   101|
   102|## Understanding the AI Landscape
   103|
   104|Before diving into implementation, let's demystify some key terms:
   105|
   106|**Artificial Intelligence (AI):** The broad field of creating machines that can perform tasks requiring human intelligence.
   107|
   108|**Machine Learning (ML):** A subset of AI where systems learn from data to improve their performance on a specific task without being explicitly programmed.
   109|
   110|**Natural Language Processing (NLP):** AI's ability to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
   111|
   112|**Computer Vision:** AI's ability to interpret and make decisions based on visual information from images and videos.
   113|
   114|**Robotic Process Automation (RPA):** Software robots that automate repetitive, rule-based digital tasks.
   115|
   116|For most small business applications, you'll be working with pre-built AI tools that incorporate these technologies behind the scenes—meaning you benefit from sophisticated AI without needing to understand the technical details.
   117|
   118|## Is Your Business Ready for AI?
   119|
   120|You don't need to be a tech expert to benefit from AI, but certain foundations make implementation smoother:
   121|
   122|✅ **Digital Presence:** You have a website, social media accounts, or use digital tools for operations  
   123|✅ **Data Collection:** You collect customer information, sales data, or operational metrics (even if it's in spreadsheets)  
   124|✅ **Pain Points:** You have specific, repetitive tasks that consume significant time  
   125|✅ **Growth Mindset:** You're open to trying new approaches to improve your business  
   126|
   127|If you checked most of these boxes, you're ready to begin your AI journey. If not, don't worry—we'll cover how to build these foundations as we go.
   128|
   129|## The Implementation Approach
   130|
   131|Throughout this book, we'll follow a proven four-phase approach to AI implementation:
   132|
   133|1. **Assess:** Identify your biggest time sinks and opportunities for improvement
   134|2. **Choose:** Select the right AI tools for your specific needs and budget
   135|3. **Implement:** Set up and configure your chosen solutions with minimal disruption
   136|4. **Optimize:** Measure results, gather feedback, and refine your approach
   137|
   138|Each chapter will guide you through one or more of these phases, building toward a comprehensive AI strategy for your business.
   139|
   140|## Real Impact: What to Expect
   141|
   142|Let's set realistic expectations for what AI can achieve in a small business context:
   143|
   144|**Time Savings:** Most small business owners report saving 5-15 hours per week after implementing AI for routine tasks like email sorting, appointment scheduling, and basic customer inquiries.
   145|
   146|**Cost Reduction:** AI can reduce operational costs by 20-30% in areas like customer service, inventory management, and marketing through automation and optimization.
   147|
   148|**Revenue Growth:** Personalized marketing, improved customer service, and better forecasting often translate to 10-25% increases in sales and customer retention.
   149|
   150|**Competitive Advantage:** Small businesses using AI effectively can compete with larger companies by offering more personalized, responsive, and efficient services.
   151|
   152|These aren't theoretical numbers—they're results achieved by real small businesses using the approaches outlined in this book.
   153|
   154|## Your AI Journey Starts Now
   155|
   156|The best time to start implementing AI in your business was yesterday. The second-best time is today. You don't need to overhaul your entire operation overnight. In fact, we recommend starting small—pick one pain point, implement one solution, measure the results, and build from success.
   157|
   158|As you work through this book, remember that perfection isn't the goal. Progress is. Each small improvement compounds over time, leading to significant transformations in how your business operates.
   159|
   160|Let's begin by examining where your time and energy are currently going—and where AI could make the biggest impact.

   165|# Chapter 2: Assessing Your Business Needs

   167|## The Importance of Starting with Assessment
   168|
   169|Before diving into specific AI tools or technologies, it's crucial to understand exactly where AI can make the biggest impact in your business. Jumping straight to implementation without proper assessment often leads to wasted time, money, and frustration on solutions that don't address your real pain points.
   170|
   171|Think of AI assessment like a medical diagnosis: you wouldn't prescribe treatment without first understanding the symptoms. Similarly, you shouldn't implement AI solutions without first identifying where your business is experiencing the most friction, inefficiency, or missed opportunities.
   172|
   173|## Conducting a Time Audit
   174|
   175|One of the most effective ways to identify AI opportunities is to conduct a thorough time audit of your daily and weekly activities. This involves tracking how you and your employees spend your time over a representative period (typically one week).
   176|
   177|### How to Conduct a Time Audit:
   178|
   179|1. **Choose Your Tracking Period:** Select a typical week that represents your normal business operations (avoid unusually busy or slow periods).
   180|
   181|2. **Create Time Categories:** Break down your work into meaningful categories such as:
   182|   - Customer service/inquiries
   183|   - Sales and lead follow-up
   184|   - Marketing content creation
   185|   - Social media management
   186|   - Email management
   187|   - Appointment scheduling
   188|   - Invoice processing and bookkeeping
   189|   - Inventory management
   190|   - Data entry and report generation
   191|   - Meetings and internal communication
   192|   - Strategic planning and business development
   193|   - Administrative tasks
   194|
   195|3. **Track Your Time:** Use a simple spreadsheet, time-tracking app, or even a notebook to record how much time you spend in each category throughout the day. Be as specific as possible—note not just what you did, but how long it took and how repetitive or tedious it felt.
   196|
   197|4. **Analyze the Results:** At the end of the week, calculate the total time spent in each category. Look for patterns:
   198|   - Which activities consume the most time?
   199|   - Which tasks feel repetitive or monotonous?
   200|   - Where do you frequently feel interrupted or unable to focus on higher-value work?
   201|   - Which tasks do you dread or procrastinate on?
   202|
   203|### Time Audit Exercise:
   204|
   205|You can't automate what you haven't measured. Before you buy any AI tool, spend three days tracking exactly how you spend your time. Most business owners overestimate how much time they spend on "important" work and underestimate the drain from repetitive tasks. This exercise reveals where your hours actually go — and once you see the numbers in black and white, the AI opportunities become obvious. Print this table, keep it on your desk, and fill it in as you go. Don't rely on memory at the end of the day; you'll miss half of it.
   206|
   207|For the next three workdays, track your time using this simple framework:
   208|
   209|| Time Period | Activity | Category | Duration (min) | Repetitive? (Y/N) | Energy Level (1-5) |

   212|| 9:30-10:00  | Creating social media posts | Marketing | 30 | Y | 3 |
   213|| ...         | ...      | ...      | ...            | ...               | ...                 |
   214|
   215|At the end of each day, review your entries and highlight:
   216|- Activities marked as repetitive (Y)
   217|- Activities with low energy levels (1-2)
   218|- Activities consuming more than 2 hours daily
   219|
   220|These are your prime candidates for AI intervention.
   221|
   222|## Identifying Pain Points and Opportunities
   223|
   224|Beyond time tracking, look for these common signs that AI could help your business:
   225|
   226|### Customer Service Bottlenecks:
   227|- Repeatedly answering the same questions
   228|- Customers complaining about slow response times
   229|- Missed inquiries outside business hours
   230|- High volume of simple, routine questions
   231|
   232|### Sales and Marketing Inefficiencies:
   233|- Leads falling through the cracks due to poor follow-up
   234|- Difficulty personalizing marketing at scale
   235|- Inconsistent social media presence
   236|- Challenges tracking campaign effectiveness
   237|
   238|### Operational Headaches:
   239|- Manual data entry errors
   240|- Inventory stockouts or overstock situations
   241|- Scheduling conflicts and double-bookings
   242|- Time-consuming invoice processing
   243|- Difficulty extracting insights from business data
   244|
   245|### Growth Constraints:
   246|- Unable to take on more customers due to capacity limits
   247|- Knowledge silos where only certain employees can perform specific tasks
   248|- Inconsistent service quality depending on who's working
   249|- Difficulty training new employees quickly

   251|## Case Study: The Local Bakery
   252|
   253|**Business:** Sweet Rose Bakery, a family-owned bakery with 3 employees and two locations.
   254|
   255|**Challenge:** Owner Maria was spending 20+ hours per week on administrative tasks, leaving little time for product development or customer interaction.
   256|
   257|**Time Audit Findings:**
   258|Maria's time audit revealed she was spending 8 hours per week on phone orders and inquiries, 5 hours per week on inventory management and supplier coordination, 4 hours per week on social media management and marketing, and 3 hours per week on bookkeeping and payroll.

   261|Maria's team implemented a phone AI assistant to handle orders and common questions, paired with inventory prediction software integrated directly with their POS system. They automated social media scheduling with AI-powered content suggestions and adopted AI-enhanced bookkeeping for automated expense categorization.
   262|
   263|**Results:**
   264|The bakery reduced administrative time by 15 hours per week, freeing up 10 hours per week for product development. Ingredient waste dropped by 22% through better forecasting, and customer response time improved from hours to just minutes.
   265|
   266|## Prioritizing AI Opportunities
   267|
   268|Not all AI opportunities are created equal. Use this framework to prioritize where to start:
   269|
   270|### The Impact/Effort Matrix:
   271|
   272|Here's where you turn your time audit into a real plan. Not every good idea deserves your attention first. The Impact/Effort Matrix forces you to rank your AI opportunities by the only two questions that matter: how much will this move the needle, and how hard is it to pull off? Focus on the high-impact, low-effort wins first — those are the projects that build momentum and buy you credibility with your team. The scoring system below gives you a numerical way to compare apples-to-oranges opportunities, so you can stop guessing and start prioritizing with confidence.
   273|
   274|Plot each potential AI application on a grid with:
   275|- **X-axis:** Implementation Effort (Low to High)
   276|- **Y-axis:** Potential Impact (Low to High)
   277|
   278|**Focus first on:** High Impact, Low Effort projects (quick wins)
   279|**Then consider:** High Impact, High Effort projects (strategic initiatives)
   280|**Avoid or defer:** Low Impact projects regardless of effort
   281|
   282|### Scoring System:
   283|
   284|For each potential AI application, score it on:
   285|1. **Time Savings Potential** (1-5): How much time could this save weekly?
   286|2. **Cost Reduction Potential** (1-5): How much could this reduce expenses?
   287|3. **Revenue Impact Potential** (1-5): How much could this increase sales?

   295|## Opportunity Identification Exercise:

   307|## Understanding Your Data Readiness
   308|
   309|AI systems learn from data, so understanding what data you have available is crucial for successful implementation.
   310|
   311|### Types of Business Data:

   360|## Setting Clear Objectives

   362|For each AI opportunity you're considering, define specific, measurable objectives:
   363|
